text.p: Gold and copper prices slipped but wheat prices rose in overnight trading. Oil prices were little changed. The CRB index was down 1.35 points at 242.3.

Copper prices trended lower during Tuesday LME trading, although the focus of attention was mostly on the wide nearby spreads as the market continued to work through fierce prompt tightness, traders said.

Spot premiums, as well as the overall spread structure, remain firm, and this trend will be maintained in the run-up towards next week's February option declarations and third Wednesday pricing two weeks after that, they said.

Cash/one day traded at a premium of $24, just $2 under the permissible daily limit, as major shorts between now and next week continue to be squeezed. Cash/one week traded at $110, while cash/February was a steep $265 traded.
The overall cash/threes backwardation was at $330/340 - equal to the levels reached during the Sumitomo-induced tightness of May last year and December 1995.
Meanwhile, the 9,650-tonne rise in LME stocks came as no surprise, given the extent of the backwardation. Metal flowed into several delivery points, attracted by the high premiums.

Forward business was uncertain, and prices drifted lower, with three months finally ending at $2,244 a tonne, a $3 loss from Monday's kerb. The market is expected to remain hamstrung between $2,230 and $2,280 overhead, they added.
Aluminium prices were unable to benefit from the welcome 6,950-tonne fall in stocks, although there was important support on dips towards $1,625 - the recent upside breakout level on the charts.
In the short-term, traders expect prices to re-challenge the $1,640 technical objective. Last business today was at $1,632, down $9 from the overnight kerb.

Nickel prices were pushed lower by the general trend, despite a 216-tonne stock decline, with business whippy at times. However, prices were defended on dips, with charts looking constructive after recent gains, and last trade was at $7,220, still down $80 from Monday.

Lead eased back to its lowest levels since early-December last year, ignoring a 775-tonne stock fall. Some traders said the market's fundamental outlook is not particularly good, as the winter draws on in the Northern Hemisphere without too much impact in the replacement battery sector. Last business was at $675, down $22 from yesterday.

Zinc business slowed during the afternoon, with prices holding nearer the lower end of the day's range. The earlier 675-tonne inventory increase did not help the market. Last trade was at $1,132, against Monday's $1,139 close.

New York precious metals futures steadied at sharply lower levels as the dollar surged higher and US stock and bond markets recovered some lost ground. Bullion was quoted at US$353.15 an ounce compared with the London afternoon fix of $353.70. "After four days in which gold recovered about $10.00 and silver about 30 cents, it looks like it's give back day," said Pell Brothers floor trader Don Tierney.
GRAINS - Wheat closed two to three cents per bushel higher amid hopes of U.S. export business to India and Egypt. Continued dry weather in wheat growing areas also supported the market.

OIL - NYMEX crude prices slipped on Tuesday afternoon but were rangebound as expectations for this evening's weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) failed to provide market direction. March crude closed off four cents at US$23.90 a barrel.
